title: The Rock, the Toll and the Legend
subtitle: St. Goar → the Loreley → Bacharach → Burg Stahleck
intro: One boat, one town, one hill — and a legend that was invented about the place you end up standing in. On the water at 1:20, land at 2:30, climb at 5:40, and let the sun go down at 8:24 from the best terrace on the Rhine. Nothing after the boat is fixed.

dayGlance.title: Up the Gorge
dayGlance.sub: 1:20 PM — the Loreley, then the toll castles.

dayGlance.title: Bacharach

dayGlance.title: The Hill & the Light

actsLede: One afternoon, four acts, water to sunset.

acts.label: Act 1 · Up the gorge
acts.tagline: Seventy minutes against the current, past the most famous rock in Germany.
acts.narrative:
Open at the pier, before you board, with Burg Katz on the hill opposite. Then the boat turns upstream and you have barely six minutes before the Loreley comes up on your left — the rock is only a kilometre away. Do not sit down.

The thing to land: the Loreley is not an old legend. Nobody in the Middle Ages told stories about a girl on that rock. A writer called Clemens Brentano made her up in 1801, in a ballad titled 'Zu Bacharach am Rheine' — Bacharach on the Rhine. He set the story in the exact town this boat is taking you to. So say it on the water and pay it off on land.

acts.label: Act 2 · Who owned the river
acts.tagline: Every castle you can see is a tollbooth.
acts.narrative:
This is the part that makes the whole valley make sense. There are more castles per mile here than anywhere in the world, and it is not romance — it is money. There was no Germany, just dozens of small rulers, and each one owned a stretch of the only motorway in Europe. Stop the boats, take a cut, let them go.

Oberwesel and Schönburg first, then Kaub — where a castle sits in the middle of the water for no reason except to collect a toll, and never once got taken.

acts.label: Act 3 · The town the legend was written about
acts.tagline: Timber-fronted houses, a wall that survived, and the wine that paid for it.
acts.narrative:
You land at half past two in the town named in the title of that 1801 poem. Eat first, properly — you have nowhere to be.

Then the town itself, and one idea holding it together: wine. Bacharach was one of the great wine names of Europe, and wine from the whole region got shipped out under its name because that name sold. The walls, the towers, the 1368 house, the four-storey church — all of it is wine money that never got knocked down.

acts.label: Act 4 · Up the hill, into the light
acts.tagline: A chapel built on a lie, a castle rebuilt from rubble, and the last hour of sun.
acts.narrative:
One climb, three beats, and they are on the same path so there is no doubling back.

The Wernerkapelle first, and do not soften it: it is a beautiful ruin built to venerate a boy whose 1287 death was blamed on Jews — an accusation that was invented and completely untrue — and what followed was a wave of massacres up and down this river. Say that plainly and move on. Then Stahleck — blown up by the French in 1689, ruined for two hundred years, rebuilt in the 1920s, a youth hostel now. Then stop talking and shoot the light.

kit: Phone or camera plus a spare battery — you're out from 1 PM until after dark
A clip mic or AirPods — the boat deck is windy and loud
Shoes for a steep 25-minute climb on cobbles and steps
A layer for the evening — it drops fast once the sun goes off the gorge
Card and some cash: KD ticket, lunch, wine. The chapel and the hill are free.
preTrip: Buy the KD ticket at the St. Goar kiosk when you arrive — a single upstream leg doesn't need pre-booking
At lunch, check DB Navigator for the last useful train to Köln, then set an alarm 30 minutes before it
Ask at the Stahleck desk whether day visitors can use the terrace — if not, the public viewpoint below is free and it's the same view
Screenshot this plan — phone signal in the gorge is patchy
goldenRule: The 13:20 boat is the only fixed time in the whole day. Be at the pier by 13:05. Everything after that bends.

days.planHeader: One boat, one town, one hill · 1:00 PM until late

planNote.text: Arrive St. Goar 1:00 PM, five minutes to the KD pier, standing there by 1:05 for the 1:20 upstream departure — into Bacharach at 2:30. Upstream is the slow direction: about 70 minutes up, 45 back down, because you're pushing against the current. After that nothing is fixed. Late lunch, the old town while the interiors are still open, wine around 5, then the climb. Golden hour starts 7:40 PM and sunset is 8:24 — be on the Stahleck terrace for both, and note that down in the town the sun drops behind the west wall of the gorge well before that. Light until roughly 9. One job over lunch: check DB Navigator for the last useful train to Köln. RB26 runs hourly to Koblenz (about 37 minutes) and on to Köln Hbf in roughly 2h15 direct, or about 1h50 if you change to an IC at Koblenz. Evening service thins out — know your last train before you climb, not after.

planArrival.title: Down the hill whenever you want
planArrival.note: Twenty minutes down to the Marktplatz, eight more to the Bahnhof. Dinner in town first if you fancy it — the whole point of tonight is that nothing is chasing you. Just don't outrun the last train.

st-goar-pier.name: St. Goar — the KD pier
st-goar-pier.story: Film the opening here, on the stage, with the river behind you and Burg Katz up on the hill opposite. You have about fifteen minutes and you only need two. Set up the promise: a rock, a made-up legend, and the town the legend was written about — which is where this boat is going.
facts: This whole 65-kilometre stretch of river is on the UN's World Heritage list — the same protected-forever list as the Pyramids and the Grand Canyon. There are more castles packed along here than anywhere else on earth, and in a minute I'll tell you why, because it isn't romance.

That castle on the hill opposite is Burg Katz, built in 1371 by the Counts of Katzenelnbogen. They got rich doing exactly one thing: stopping boats on this river and charging them to carry on. 'Katz' is just short for the family name.
We're going upstream, against the current — that's why it takes seventy minutes up and only about forty-five coming back down. The Rhine here moves fast, and that matters for the next story.

routeCard.sub: KD Anlegestelle, St. Goar · be there 1:05 PM · boat 1:20
routeCard.note: Five minutes on foot from the station. KD ask you to be at the stage 15 minutes before departure — buy the ticket at the kiosk.

planCard.todo: Cold open here. The hook, the promise, done in two takes. Then get on the boat — this is the one departure you cannot miss.

loreley.name: The Loreley
loreley.angle: The legend is 225 years old, not medieval
loreley.story: It comes up on your left barely six minutes out of St. Goar — the rock is only about a kilometre upstream of the pier, so there is no settling-in period. Be outside before the boat casts off. Everyone films the rock; almost nobody knows the story is a modern invention. That's your angle — and it pays off later, because the man who invented it set it in Bacharach.
facts: A wall of slate 132 metres above the water, and right here the Rhine squeezes down to 113 metres wide — the narrowest point on the whole navigable river. Fast, deep, and it genuinely used to wreck boats. The danger was real. The girl was not.

Nobody in the Middle Ages told stories about a woman on this rock. A writer called Clemens Brentano invented her in 1801, in a ballad called 'Zu Bacharach am Rheine' — Bacharach on the Rhine. He set it in the town this boat is taking us to. We land there in an hour.

A German poet called Heinrich Heine wrote the famous version in 1824, and it became one of those poems every German child learns at school. Here's the part people don't know: when the Nazis took power they wanted it gone, because Heine was Jewish. It was too popular to ban — so they kept printing it in schoolbooks and credited it to 'author unknown'.

routeCard.sub: From the deck, left-hand side · about 1:26 PM
routeCard.note: Left-hand side going upstream, and it comes fast — roughly six minutes after casting off. Be on deck before the boat leaves, not after.

planCard.todo: Do NOT sit down when you board. The rock is up in about six minutes. Shoot it, then say the 1801 line straight to camera — that's the thread the whole video hangs on.

oberwesel.name: Oberwesel & Schönburg
oberwesel.angle: The town that kept its towers
oberwesel.story: About twenty-five minutes past the Loreley, on your right. Oberwesel is called the town of towers and you can count them from the water. Schönburg sits above it — and its story is the whole valley's story in miniature: built to tax the river, burned by the French, left as a ruin, bought back.
facts: Oberwesel kept 16 of its 21 medieval wall towers. Most Rhine towns pulled theirs down in the 1800s to make room for roads and the railway — this one didn't, and you can see the whole defensive ring from the boat.

Schönburg up there wasn't a house, it was a walled village. At its peak in the 1300s about 250 people from 24 different families lived inside it at once — the castle got subdivided between heirs until it was basically a stone tower block.

In 1689 it was burned down by the army of the French king Louis XIV, who sent his soldiers up this valley to torch it town by town. It stayed a ruin for about 200 years, until a German-American businessman spent a fortune rebuilding it before 1914. The town bought it back off his son in 1950.

routeCard.sub: From the deck, right-hand side · about 1:50 PM
routeCard.note: Right-hand side going upstream. Schönburg is the castle on the hill above the town.

see: The medieval wall and its towers
The Liebfrauenkirche, red against the hill
planCard.todo: Swap to the right-hand rail. Count the towers on camera — it's a better line than reciting the number.

kaub.name: Kaub — Pfalzgrafenstein & Gutenfels
kaub.angle: A castle parked in the middle of a river to take your money
kaub.story: The best five minutes on the water, about fifteen minutes before you land. A stone ship moored midstream with a castle on the hill behind it — a two-part trap, and the clearest possible picture of what every castle in this valley was actually for.
facts: That white castle sitting in the middle of the river is called Pfalzgrafenstein, and it was built in 1326 by the man who was king of Germany at the time, Ludwig of Bavaria. It had exactly one purpose: a chain stretched across the water, and a toll. Pay, or you don't go past. It was still taking money off passing boats until 1867.

And it was never taken and never destroyed — the only castle on this river you can say that about. Everything else here got burned at some point. It survived because it sits on a rock in a fast river and nobody could be bothered.

One more thing happened right here. Napoleon had spent years conquering most of Europe, and in 1813 he finally lost a massive battle in Germany and began retreating home to France. On New Year's night, a general from Prussia — the state that later grew into Germany — chased him across the Rhine at this exact spot, over a floating bridge of boats tied to that island. Fifty to sixty thousand men, fifteen thousand horses and 182 cannon, over several days.

routeCard.sub: From the deck, left-hand side · about 2:14 PM
routeCard.note: Left-hand side going upstream. Pfalzgrafenstein is mid-river; Gutenfels is the castle on the hill above Kaub.

planCard.todo: Best shot of the boat trip. Get it wide first, then talk over it: the chain, the toll, never taken. Then start packing up — Bacharach is 15 minutes off.

lunch.name: Late lunch, Bacharach
lunch.story: The pier is about five minutes from the market square. Sit somewhere you can see the old timber-fronted houses and take the full hour — the rest of the day has no deadlines in it.

routeCard.sub: Marktplatz, Bacharach · 5 minutes from the landing stage
routeCard.note: Walk in off the pier, under the railway, and you're in the old town.

planCard.todo: Eat properly. While you're sitting down, open DB Navigator and pick your last train home — that's the only admin of the day.

old-town.name: The old town & the walls
old-town.angle: Wine money that never got knocked down
old-town.story: Bacharach is small enough to walk in twenty minutes and it still has almost its entire medieval wall. That's the unusual bit — most Rhine towns demolished theirs in the 1800s for roads and the railway. Here they just built around it.
facts: Nearly the whole medieval town wall is still standing, with its towers and gates. Walk out to the edge and you can put your hand on it. Most towns this size lost theirs 200 years ago.
The name: you'll be told it comes from 'Bacchi ara' — the altar of Bacchus, the Roman god of wine. That's a lovely story somebody invented much later. The wine part, though, is completely true.

Bacharach was one of the biggest wine names in Europe. Wine from all over the region got shipped out from this quay under Bacharach's name, because that name sold better than the name of wherever it actually came from. Everything you're looking at was paid for by that.

routeCard.sub: Marktplatz and the walls · 3:30 PM · free
routeCard.note: A loop of about twenty minutes if you don't stop. Do it slowly instead.

walkPoints.name: Marktplatz
walkPoints.story: The market square — Marktplatz, if you're reading a sign. It was the centre of the wine trade, and it's still the centre of the town.
walkPoints.todo: Start here. Wide shot of the square before it fills up.

walkPoints.name: The town wall & Marktturm
walkPoints.story: Nearly the full medieval ring, towers and gates included — unusual on the Rhine.
walkPoints.todo: Walk a stretch of it. Good place to say the wine-money line.

walkPoints.name: The Rhine quay
walkPoints.story: Where the wine actually left from, and where you landed an hour ago.
walkPoints.todo: Look back at the river you came up. Nice cutaway.

planCard.todo: Loose walking segment. One idea only: this town is wine money that survived. Don't over-film it — the good stuff is later.

altes-haus.name: Altes Haus (1368)
altes-haus.angle: The postcard, and why it's still standing
altes-haus.story: The oldest house in town and the shot everyone comes for. It's what people call half-timbered — you can see the dark wooden beams criss-crossing the front with pale plaster filled in between. Worth thirty seconds on how that actually works, because it explains why a building that visibly leans has been fine for six and a half centuries.
facts: Built in 1368 — the oldest house in Bacharach. It's been standing for well over 650 years and it's a restaurant now.

Those criss-crossing beams aren't decoration — the wooden frame is the entire structure of the house, and everything between the beams is just filling. It's a skeleton, not a wall. That's why it can lean and twist as the wood moves over the centuries and still hold itself up.
In 1689 French troops blew up the castle and the chapel on the hill above. Down here, the houses came through. This one has outlived that war and every one since.

routeCard.sub: Oberstraße 61, Bacharach · 4:00 PM · free from outside
routeCard.note: Two minutes off the market square. Best light on the front is later in the afternoon, which is when you'll be there.

planCard.todo: Get the clean front-on shot first, then talk. The frame-is-the-structure point is the one worth saying.

st-peters.name: St. Peter's Church
st-peters.angle: Watch the architecture change as you look up
st-peters.story: Two hundred years to build, and you can see every one of them. Start at the bottom with the heavy round arches and follow your eye up until they go pointed. It's a building that changes style halfway through, in public.
facts: They started it around 1100 and didn't finish until the 1300s. Look at the bottom: round, heavy arches — that's Romanesque. Now look up: pointed arches, taller windows — that's Gothic. Same building, two hundred years apart.

The main hall you walk into — the long tall bit, which architects call the nave — is four storeys high. That is unusually tall, and unusually expensive, for a church in a town this small. Wine money again.

It's a Protestant church, and has been for roughly 500 years. Before that, western Europe had one single Catholic church, until a huge religious split called the Reformation broke it in two. The rule that ended the fighting was blunt: whichever side the local ruler picked, everyone living in his territory had to follow. The ruler here picked Protestant — so the town became Protestant.

routeCard.sub: Blücherstraße, by the market square · 4:20 PM · free
routeCard.note: Interiors on the Rhine usually shut around 6 PM — get inside before then, because after that you're on the hill.

planCard.todo: Film a slow tilt up the nave — the shot does the explaining for you. This is the last interior of the day, so don't skip it.

riesling.name: A glass of Riesling on the square
riesling.angle: Do this now, not squeezed against a train
riesling.story: Sit down in the square with a glass of the local white while the town is still busy. This is deliberately before the climb, not after — coming down hot at half eight and rushing a drink would waste the scene.
facts: This is Riesling country and has been for centuries. The vines grow on slate terraces so steep they have to be worked by hand — no machine can get up them.
The slate is the point: it holds the day's heat and pushes it back at the grapes overnight, and it's where that flinty, mineral edge in the glass is supposed to come from.
There's far less of it than there used to be. Hand-working a vertical vineyard doesn't pay, so terraces up and down this valley have gone back to scrub. What's in the glass is a shrinking thing.

routeCard.note: Any of the wine bars round the square — Weinstube is the word you'll see on the signs. Pick one with outside tables facing the church.

see: A glass of Middle Rhine Riesling
planCard.todo: Sit down properly. One relaxed piece to camera about the slate and the hand-worked terraces, then put the phone away for ten minutes.

wernerkapelle.name: The Wernerkapelle
wernerkapelle.angle: The prettiest ruin on the hill is a monument to a lie
wernerkapelle.story:
It's on the path up to the castle, so you pass it whether you plan to or not. Don't film it as scenery. It is a beautiful unfinished stone shell — pointed arches, empty windows, no roof — and it exists because of an accusation that got people killed. The honest thirty seconds you spend on that will be the strongest part of the video.

Say it simply, don't editorialise, don't linger. Then keep walking.
facts: In 1287 a boy was found dead near here. Jews were blamed, on the basis of what's called a blood libel — the false claim that Jews murdered Christian children to use their blood. It was never true. Not here, not anywhere.

What followed was a wave of massacres — mobs going through Jewish streets killing people — right along this river and the river Moselle next door. Entire communities were wiped out. This chapel was begun in 1289 to honour the dead boy as a saint, and people were still working on it in the 1430s. It was never finished.

And this isn't safely buried in the past. The Catholic Church kept that boy on its official list of local saints until 1963. A stone carving showing the murder that never happened, on the sister chapel downriver at Oberwesel, only came down in 1970.

routeCard.sub: On the castle path above the town · 5:55 PM · free, open ruin
routeCard.note: About 15 minutes uphill from the market square, and directly on the way to the castle — no detour. Steps and a steady climb from here on.

see: Empty window frames against the sky
planCard.todo: Shoot it, then say the 1287 story straight and plainly — no music, no drama. Thirty seconds. Then move on up the hill and let it sit.

stahleck.name: Burg Stahleck
stahleck.angle: Blown up, forgotten for 200 years, now a youth hostel
stahleck.story: Twenty-five minutes of steady climbing from the town and the view arrives all at once. The castle is the seat of the men who ran this stretch of the Rhine, and what happened to it afterwards is almost funnier than its history.
facts: Twelfth century, and it belonged to the family who ran this entire stretch of the Rhine. Their title was Count Palatine — which sounds grand and just means a count who governed on the king's behalf. It made him one of the most powerful men in Germany. And that castle you saw sitting out in the river? Pfalzgrafenstein. The name literally means 'the Count Palatine's rock' — same title, same job: control the river, take the money.
French soldiers blew it up in 1689 — the same army that burned Schönburg and wrecked the chapel you just walked past. It sat as a heap of rubble for over two hundred years.
It was rebuilt in the 1920s and it's been a youth hostel ever since. You can sleep in a Rhine castle for about the price of a pizza — and the terrace has the best view on the Middle Rhine.

routeCard.sub: Above Bacharach · 6:40 PM · 15 min further up from the chapel
routeCard.note: Another 10–15 minutes of steps up from the chapel (about 25 minutes if you climbed straight from the town). There's a bistro and terrace with cheap beer and wine — ask at the desk whether day visitors can use it. If not, the public viewpoint just below is free and it's the same gorge.

planCard.todo: Arrive, get your breath, then film the reveal of the view before you say anything. Settle in — you're staying up here for the light.

golden-hour.name: Golden hour & sunset from the terrace
golden-hour.angle: The closing shot — and the reason you're up here
golden-hour.story: This is why the day got rearranged. Golden hour starts at 7:40 and the sun goes down at 8:24, and from up here you keep the light long after the streets below have gone into shadow — the gorge walls take the sun off the town first. Stop talking, shoot it, and sign off when it's nearly gone.
facts: Sunset tonight is 8:24 PM, golden hour runs from about 7:40, and it stays properly light until around 9. Down in the town the sun disappears behind the west wall of the gorge well before that — which is the entire reason to be standing up here instead.
From this terrace you can see the whole shape of the day at once: the river you came up, the toll castles downstream, the hand-worked terraces, and the town the Loreley legend was written about.
And that's the whole day in one view: up the river past the castles that taxed it, into the town where the legend was written, and up here above all of it watching the light go.

routeCard.sub: Stahleck terrace or the viewpoint below · 7:30–8:30 PM · free
routeCard.note: Sunset 8:24 PM, light until roughly 9. Bring the layer — it drops quickly once the sun is off the gorge.

see: The gorge in shadow below you
Lights coming on in the town
planCard.todo: Closing shot of the episode. Film the light first, talk second. Get a long steady wide of the valley — that's what the outro plays over.

bahnhof.name: Bacharach Bahnhof
bahnhof.angle: Home when you feel like it
bahnhof.story: Twenty minutes down the hill to the market square, eight more to the station. Dinner in town first if you want it.

routeCard.sub: Bacharach Bf — the railway station · about 8 minutes from the market square
routeCard.note: RB26 hourly to Koblenz (about 37 min), on to Köln Hbf in roughly 2h15 direct — or about 1h50 changing to an IC at Koblenz. Evening service thins out: use the last train you checked at lunch.

planCard.todo: Nothing left to film. Eat if you're hungry, then take the train you picked at lunchtime.

coldOpen.title: Cold open
coldOpen.where: The KD pier, St. Goar — 1:10 PM
facts: The hook: 'the most famous rock in Germany is behind me, and the legend attached to it is younger than the United States'
What this is: one boat ride, one town, one hill. Up the Rhine gorge past the castles that taxed it, into the town the Loreley was invented about.
The promise: 'and we finish at sunset, on a terrace above all of it'

signOff.title: Closing sign-off
facts: Where you are: on the hill above the town that the Loreley poem was set in, watching the light go off the river you came up this afternoon
The shape of the day: on the water at 1:20, in the town at 2:30, on this hill at 6:15, and the sun going at 8:24. One valley, seven hundred years of people charging money to pass through it.
The ask: like, subscribe — and where should the next one go?

talkTipbox: Assume your viewer knows none of this — and assume you don't either until you've said it out loud once. Every single time a name comes up, give one plain line on who or what that is before you carry on: not 'the Count Palatine' but 'the man who ran this stretch of river for the king'. Same for places, same for dates. Three facts a stop, and you only need the one that grabbed you. What happened, when, and why it's surprising. The Wernerkapelle is the exception — say that one plainly, no flourish, and don't rush it.
goldenRules: The 13:20 boat is the only fixed time all day. Be at the pier by 13:05.
Miss it and the 14:20 still works — you're not chasing a train tonight.
Going upstream: the Loreley is up in SIX minutes, on your left. Kaub also left; Oberwesel and Schönburg on your right.
St. Peter's and any other interior before 6 PM. After that you're on the hill.
Don't rush the Wernerkapelle. Thirty honest seconds beats a minute of hedging.
Golden hour 7:40, sunset 8:24, light until about 9. Be up top for all of it.
Check the last train to Köln over lunch, not at 8 PM.
outro: The legend was written about this town. You arrive by water, climb above it, and watch the light go. That's an ending.
